title: How do we draw a rectangle with sides four and six centimetres?
description: A rectangle with sides four centimetres and six centimetres is drawn from one side and two perpendiculars. The finished drawing is checked for both properties of a rectangle: opposite sides equal, and every angle ninety degrees.
teaching_notes: One idea: draw the base, stand a perpendicular at each end, mark the second length on each, join, then check both properties. Watch for students who join the tops before drawing the perpendiculars, or who skip the check.

video_script.why: A learner draws a rectangle from two side lengths and checks both properties of a rectangle.
video_script.substitution: the same way as the example in your book: a base, a perpendicular at each end, then the top joined across
video_script.anchor: a rectangle being drawn on the board from a base and two upright lines
video_script.payoff_line: Both properties of a rectangle hold.

final_answer.value: Rectangle ABCD with AB = CD = 4 cm, AD = BC = 6 cm, all angles 90°. Both properties hold

maths_rules: perpendiculars at A and B, with AD = 6 cm and BC = 6 cm
DC joined; DC = 4 cm = AB and AD = BC = 6 cm, so opposite sides are equal
angle A = angle B = angle C = angle D = 90°
video_script.design: A rectangle is drawn in a fixed order on the board, then the two properties are checked on the finished drawing.

narration: <bookmark mark='props'/>A rectangle has two properties that we can check on any drawing.
The first property is that opposite sides are equal in length.
<bookmark mark='second'/>The second property is that all the angles are right angles.
<bookmark mark='plan'/>To draw it, we fix one side and stand a perpendicular at each end.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a rectangle with sides four centimetres and six centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: draw a perpendicular at A and at B; mark D with AD = 6 cm and C with BC = 6 cm

<bookmark mark='markc'/>On the one at bee, mark cee so that bee cee is six centimetres.
